passage: "What if the storm breaks the window? What if the thunder comes inside? What if you don't wake up?" Five-year-old Hiroshi asks in their Osaka flat, clutching his quilt. His mother, Dalia, doesn't say, "Don't be silly." She sits on the bed. "The window is strong glass. Thunder is only a sound. I'll be in the next room, and I'll check on you when I go to bed, like always." Then she does the same three things as every night: water glass, night-light, one song. Hiroshi asks one more what-if, quieter. By the second verse, his grip loosens.

qa.q: What three things does Dalia do every night?
qa.a: Water glass, night-light, one song.

qa.q: What does Hiroshi clutching his quilt suggest he feels?
qa.a: He is frightened; the storm worries feel real and big to him.

qa.q: What choice did Dalia make instead of telling Hiroshi not to be silly?
qa.a: She gave calm, simple answers and kept the same bedtime steps, which soothed him.

qa.q: What would change if Dalia had said there was nothing to fear and left?
qa.a: Hiroshi would likely feel his worry was not heard and lie awake more frightened.

grounding: A young child asks what-if questions about a storm at bedtime, and his mother's calm answers and familiar routine soothe him.

passage: At nap time in the daycare, Anjali, five, lies stiff on her mat with her eyes open. "What if Mumma is late today? What if the bus breaks? What if she forgets me?" Urmila, the carer, kneels beside her. "Mumma comes at five. When the big hand is on the twelve, the gate bell rings. If she's ever late, I stay with you until she comes. Every time." Anjali asks the same questions again, and Urmila answers them the same way, calmly. Then Urmila pats the mat three times, their nap signal. Anjali's eyes close. At five, the bell rings.

qa.q: What is Urmila and Anjali's nap signal?
qa.a: Urmila pats the mat three times.

qa.q: What is Anjali worried about as she lies stiff on her mat?
qa.a: She fears her Mumma will be late or forget her.

qa.q: What did Urmila do when Anjali asked the same questions again?
qa.a: Urmila answered them the same way, calmly, and gave the usual nap signal, which helped Anjali rest.

qa.q: How might Anjali's Mumma feel on hearing how Urmila handled the worry?
qa.a: She may feel grateful that her daughter was comforted rather than hushed.

grounding: A worried child asks what-if questions about her mother being late, and a carer's calm, repeated answers and routine soothe her.

passage:
Note for Maria's parents, Friday night
Maria went to bed at eight but asked lots of what-ifs. What if the storm breaks the window? What if you don't come back from the wedding? At first I said, 'There's nothing to be scared of,' and she cried harder. So I tried something else. I showed her the window latch and let her check it herself. I told her you'd be home after she was asleep and would kiss her goodnight. We did your bedtime steps exactly: story, water, night light. She fell asleep holding my hand.
Vandana

qa.q: What did Maria ask about the storm?
qa.a: What if the storm breaks the window?

qa.q: Why did Maria cry harder when told there was nothing to be scared of?
qa.a: Her worry felt real and big, so being told there was nothing to fear left her feeling unheard.

qa.q: Which of Vandana's steps helped Maria settle?
qa.a: Letting her check the window latch, telling her calmly when her parents would be back, and following the usual bedtime steps.

qa.q: How might Maria's parents feel reading the note?
qa.a: They would likely feel grateful and reassured that Maria's worries were taken seriously and her routine was kept.

grounding: Shows, in a sitter's note, a child full of bedtime what-ifs who is soothed by calm answers and a familiar routine, not by being told there is nothing to fear.

passage: Rain drummed on the tin roof, and Abbu was late back from the mandi. Hafsa sat up on the charpai again. 'What if the bus fell in the river? What if a snake comes in?' Vidya aunty from next door didn't laugh. She lit the lantern and sat close. 'The bus goes on the high road, and the bridge is strong. The door has a stopper at the bottom. Shall we check?' They checked together. Then Vidya aunty sang the rhyme Hafsa always had at bedtime. Hafsa's eyes closed halfway through. Later the gate creaked: Abbu, wet and smiling.

qa.q: Where was Abbu coming back from?
qa.a: From the mandi.

qa.q: What was Hafsa worried about?
qa.a: She was frightened that the bus might fall in the river or a snake might come in while Abbu was late in the rain.

qa.q: What did Vidya aunty do that soothed Hafsa?
qa.a: She took the worries seriously, gave calm facts, checked the door with her, and sang the usual bedtime rhyme.

qa.q: How might Abbu feel coming home to find Hafsa asleep?
qa.a: He would probably feel relieved and grateful that she was calm and cared for while he was late.

grounding: Shows a child asking frightened what-if questions at bedtime while a parent is late, soothed by calm answers and a familiar routine.

passage: In their flat in Leeds, Zeynep lay stiff under the duvet. 'Baba, what if there's a monster under the bed? What if it comes when you're asleep?' Yosef didn't say, 'Monsters aren't real.' Last week that had only made her cry. Instead he knelt, lifted the edge of the sheet and shone the torch. 'Just your slippers and a sock.' Then the usual: two pages of the whale book, night light on, door open a hand's width. 'I'll peek in when the clock chimes nine.' Zeynep turned on her side. At nine he peeked. She was asleep.

qa.q: What did Yosef find under the bed?
qa.a: Just her slippers and a sock.

qa.q: What was Zeynep feeling as she lay stiff under the duvet?
qa.a: She was frightened, worried that a monster might come while her father slept.

qa.q: Why did Yosef's approach work better than last week's?
qa.a: Checking with the torch and keeping the same bedtime steps calmed her, while 'Monsters aren't real' had only made her cry.

qa.q: What might these bedtimes be like for Yosef?
qa.a: He may feel tired or worried himself, but he stays patient and keeps to the routine because he knows it helps.

grounding: Shows a child's bedtime monster worries soothed by a calm check and a predictable routine rather than being told there is nothing to fear.

passage:
Nap time at the Little Stars crèche. The blinds were down, but Jomon sat up on his mat.
"Aunty Chandrika, what if a storm comes?"
"Then we'll stay inside here. It's a strong building."
"What if Appa is late?"
Chandrika knelt beside him. "What happens after nap?"
"Snack," he whispered.
"Then?"
"Painting. Then songs."
"And then Appa comes. Every day, after songs."
Jomon lay back down, still holding his blanket tight. A minute later he asked, "What if a monster—"
"Monsters don't come to the crèche," she said softly, "but I'll sit right here." She stayed, patting his back, until his breathing slowed.

qa.q: What comes after snack in Jomon's day?
qa.a: Painting, then songs.

qa.q: What was Jomon worried about at nap time?
qa.a: He felt scared that a storm might come or that Appa would be late; he kept sitting up and holding his blanket tight.

qa.q: Why did going through the day's order help Jomon?
qa.a: Saying snack, painting, songs, then Appa gave him a steady picture of what comes next, which calmed him more than being told not to worry.

qa.q: How might Chandrika see Jomon's questions?
qa.a: She treats them as real worries, not naughtiness, so she answers calmly and sits beside him until he settles.

grounding: Shows a young child with many what-if worries being soothed by calm answers and a predictable routine.
